text: Every major browser ships with built-in developer tools, and the Console tab inside them is where you'll actually debug real code — not just console.log, but errors, tables, and a live JavaScript prompt running directly against the real page in front of you. This closes out Chapter One before Chapter Two picks up the pace with modern syntax.

console.log is what every beginner reaches for first, but it's not the only tool worth knowing. console.error marks a message as an error, styled in red with a clickable stack trace showing exactly which line logged it, so you can jump straight to the source. console.table renders an array of objects as an actual table instead of a wall of text — worth knowing specifically because arrays of objects are exactly the shape most blockchain data comes in.

Press F12, or Control Shift J in Chrome, to open DevTools directly to the Console tab. It shows two things at once: anything your page's own JavaScript logs as it runs, and a live prompt sitting right below it where you can type and run JavaScript yourself, immediately, against the actual page that's open.

The console isn't just for reading output — it's a live prompt. Typing an expression and pressing Enter runs it immediately against the page you have open and prints back whatever it returns, with no need to edit a file and reload. This is how experienced developers actually debug in practice: reaching in and querying, or even modifying, a running page directly, instead of guessing and adding more log lines.

You're ready for Chapter Two once you're comfortable opening DevTools and reading what it shows you. console.log, console.error, console.table, and a live prompt that runs real JavaScript against a real page. Next up: ES6+ syntax — the modern JavaScript that every library in this course actually uses.
